edits.quote: Two players alternate taking 1 or 2 counters. Never take more than remain. Taking the last counter wins.
edits.fix: The same rules are printed in full in P1, P3 and P5. State them once as brief unnumbered shared rules at the top of page 1, in plain read-aloud words ("Take turns. On your turn take 1 or 2 counters. Whoever takes the last counter wins."), and delete them from the problems.

edits.quote: Use the same 1-or-2 rule.
edits.fix: Delete; the rule is activity-wide.

edits.quote: Play from 4 counters twice, swapping who starts. ... Play from 5 counters twice, swapping who starts. Record the moves and circle the last move.
edits.fix: These are two near-identical one-minute play-and-record tasks with no question. Merge them into one problem with a goal: "Play from 4 and from 5 counters, taking turns going first. Can the first player always win? What should the first move be?"

edits.quote: Draw or write the number taken at each turn. Circle the last move.
edits.fix: The record does not show who made each move or who won, so after swapping starters the games cannot be compared. Give each game two labelled rows (me / partner) or add a "Who won: first or second?" box, and drop the circling.

edits.quote: Start with 3 counters. Let the other player start. Try each of their first moves below. Record how many you take next. [table: Starting pile 3/3, Other player takes 1/2, I take next, Counters left]
edits.fix: This is trivial because the opponent's moves are filled in, the reply is always to take the rest, and the 'Counters left' column is always 0 ('Starting pile' only repeats the text). Rewrite as a question: "From 3 counters, would you rather go first or second? Try every way the game can go." Delete the pre-filled column and the redundant columns.

edits.quote: Start with 6 counters. Make two groups of 3. Let the other player start. Try each first move below and choose your reply so that exactly 3 counters remain. Then finish each game.
edits.fix: This prints the leave-3 strategy (and the grouping method) before P5 asks children to find traps, and the 'Counters left' column is then always 3. Replace it with: "Start with 6. Your partner goes first. Can you win every time, whatever your partner takes?" Leave out the groups and the target number.

edits.quote: Draw the two groups before the game: [large box placed after the game table]
edits.fix: Delete. It is busywork, and it sits after the table it is supposed to come before.

edits.quote: Play twice from each pile and check your choice. [table columns: Pile / I choose first or second / My first move if I start]
edits.fix: There is no space to record the six check games or whether the choice worked. Add a 'Did I win? (game 1 / game 2)' column.

edits.quote: Build 12 counters as four groups of 3. Let the other player start. After each of their moves, take enough to remove 3 counters between your two turns. Record the numbers left after each of your turns.
edits.fix: This prints the whole winning strategy, the wording 'between your two turns' is confusing, and the recorded numbers are forced (9, 6, 3, 0). Replace it with an open trap hunt: "Which piles from 1 to 15 are traps, piles you want your partner to move from? Mark them on the number strip and test each one against every move." Print a 1-15 strip.

edits.quote: Draw my four groups:
edits.fix: Delete the label and its box (busywork).

edits.quote: Packet ends after P6 with about a third of page 3 blank.
edits.fix: A quick child finishes in about 18 minutes, so about 22 minutes are missing (first block). Add a substantial problem, for example the full trap hunt to 15 described above with a printed strip, if P6 is not rewritten that way.

edits.quote: No contrasting rule anywhere in the K-1 pages.
edits.fix: Second block of missing time: add a contrasting game, for example take 1, 2 or 3 (traps at 4, 8, 12) or 'whoever takes the last counter loses', with a pile/first-or-second table. Children then see a new rule change the traps.

k-1.summary: The {1,2} games are mathematically correct and the tables are clean, but a quick child runs out of work in about 18 minutes. P4 and P6 print the leave-a-multiple-of-3 strategy that P5 should let children discover. P1-P3 are tiny play-and-record tasks with no question, so the band needs a real trap hunt and a contrasting rule.

edits.quote: a partner may write while you play
edits.fix: Delete. This is classroom logistics for the adult.

edits.quote: Winner: first or sec- ond (column header hyphenated across two lines)
edits.fix: Widen the column or shorten the header to 'Who won?' so the word is not broken.

edits.quote: Use moves 1, 3, and 4.
edits.fix: The full rules are in P1 and repeated in P3 and P5. Put 'Take turns removing 1, 3 or 4 counters; taking the last counter wins' once as unnumbered shared rules at the top of page 1, and delete the repeats.

edits.quote: Build a pile of 2, then a pile of 4. From each pile, try every allowed first move. Reset the pile before the next attempt. Record how many counters each move leaves.
edits.fix: This is a one-minute directed sub-step of the P3 chart. Delete it and renumber.

edits.quote: Work from small piles upward. List all legal next piles. Mark W if at least one is L; mark L if all are W.
edits.fix: This prints backward induction as a procedure. Keep the W/L definitions and the chart, delete the method, and leave the hint with the adult.

edits.quote: Put L at 0 because there is no move.
edits.fix: Delete; the chart already shows 0 / none / L.

edits.quote: Chart rows for piles 0-7 only
edits.fix: P6 needs labels for 8 and 9, and P7 needs piles up to 14, but there is nowhere to work them out. Extend the chart to pile 14.

edits.quote: such as 2 or 7
edits.fix: Delete; it gives away the L piles that P3 asks children to find.

edits.quote: Reset and try every different first move. Record your replies. Starting pile, each first move, and my replies: [one blank box]
edits.fix: It is unclear whether to record only the first reply or the whole game, and the strategy must answer every later reply too. Replace the box with a table: partner's first move (1 / 3 / 4), my reply, rest of the game, who won.

edits.quote: From 8 counters, try taking 1, 3, and 4. Reset each time. ... Do the same from 10.
edits.fix: These are three-row fill-ins of about two minutes each, and P7 repeats the same step a third time. Merge P5-P7 into one problem: "For each pile from 8 to 14, would you rather go first or second? If first, list every winning move."

edits.quote: not just the first one you find
edits.fix: Delete this 'not X' tic; 'Record all winning moves from 10' already says it.

edits.quote: Make a strategy card: record each possible first move and the pile it leaves. Circle moves that hand your opponent an L. Test the card in a game.
edits.fix: The card covers only the first move, an L pile (9 or 14) leaves nothing to circle, piles 10-14 are off the chart, and one game does not test every reply. Rewrite: choose first or second for your pile, and make a card that tells you what to do after every move your partner could make until the game ends. Then have the partner try to beat it.

edits.quote: Band ends after P7 with a third of page 3 blank.
edits.fix: A quick third grader finishes in about 27 minutes, so about 15 minutes are missing. Add a substantial problem, for example: "Is taking 4 (the most you can) ever a losing move? Find piles where it is", or extend the L piles to 30 and predict a large pile.

grades-2-3.summary: This is a sound backward-induction sequence on {1,3,4} with correct expected answers (L at 0, 2, 7, 9, 14), and P4 tests a strategy against every reply as the outline asks. The labelling procedure is printed, though, P2, P5 and P6 are one- or two-minute directed fill-ins, and the chart stops at 7 while later problems need piles 8-14. A quick child finishes in about 27 minutes.

edits.quote: Swap who starts for a second attempt at a pile that surprised you.
edits.fix: This is vague and there is only one spare row. Change to 'Play each pile twice, swapping who starts. Which piles would you rather start from?' and give two rows per pile.

edits.quote: Winner: first or sec- ond (column header hyphenated across two lines)
edits.fix: Widen the column or shorten the header to 'Who won?'.

edits.quote: Continue using moves 1, 3, and 4. ... Return to moves 1, 3, and 4.
edits.fix: State the {1,3,4} rules once as unnumbered shared rules at the top of page 1. Delete the reminders and let only P8 state its rule change.

edits.quote: Build small piles and work upward: mark W if a legal move reaches L, and L if every legal move reaches W.
edits.fix: This prints the backward-induction rule. Keep the W/L definitions and 'build small piles', and leave the method to the child.

edits.quote: Zero is L.
edits.fix: Delete; the chart already shows 0 / none / L.

edits.quote: Fill the chart in order. [P3 chart starts again at pile 0]
edits.fix: P3 re-labels piles 0-7, which P2 has just done (padding). Merge P2 and P3 into one chart where children record next piles for the first rows and labels or moves beyond.

edits.quote: Compare the rows after filling at least two of them. [chart drawn 7 cells wide, so L falls in the same two columns of every row]
edits.fix: The 7-wide grid plus the instruction gives away the period, which is this band's central discovery. Redraw the chart as rows of 10 (0-29) and replace the sentence with a question: 'Which piles are L? Predict the label of pile 100.'

edits.quote: Compare these four piles. Record every legal next pile and its label. Circle the starting piles that have no move to L. [rows ordered 14, 16, 15, 17]
edits.fix: This repeats checks already done in P3, and the ordering groups the two L piles first. Delete it or fold it into P3.

edits.quote: The repeating pattern I see:
edits.fix: The only pattern prompt is a box label, and the problem text never asks for it. Put the question in the P3 text: 'Describe the pattern of L piles.'

edits.quote: Arrange 14, 16, 15, and 17 counters in whole groups of 7 with a smaller leftover group. Record the leftovers. Match each pile to its label in Problem 4.
edits.fix: This hands over the mod-7 discovery as a procedure. Delete it and ask children to state their own rule for which piles are L (P3) and test it on a large pile.

edits.quote: Use your chart to choose a winning move for each leftover count marked W. Record the leftover count after the move. For counts marked L, list every leftover count an allowed move can reach; use piles 7 and 9 so that all three moves are possible.
edits.fix: The text is convoluted, the 'Move to L, or all moves from L' column mixes two tasks, and the hint (piles 7 and 9) belongs with the adult. The actual goal, why the pattern continues forever, is never stated. Rewrite as one central problem: 'Explain why every pile leaving 0 or 2 when grouped in sevens is L, no matter how large.'

edits.quote: Build 24 counters. Choose a first move using your table, then play. After each of your turns record the leftover count when grouping the remaining pile in sevens.
edits.fix: Pile 24 is already on the 0-27 chart, so the leftover idea is not needed and the recording is busywork. Use a pile beyond the chart (for example 50 or 100) and play it out against a partner.

edits.quote: Build smaller piles to check a proposed strategy. Record which piles you want to hand the other player.
edits.fix: 'A proposed strategy' does not say whose. Ask directly: 'Which piles do you want to hand the other player? Explain why that works for every pile, and compare with moves 1, 3, 4.'

edits.quote: My games and the piles I want to leave: [one box about 1 inch tall]
edits.fix: The box is too small for four games, small-pile checks and a conclusion. Enlarge it, or add a pile 0-12 label strip.

edits.quote: Change the allowed moves to 1, 3, and 5. ... Return to moves 1, 3, and 4.
edits.fix: The rule switch sits between {1,3,4} problems and forces a switch back. Move P8 to the end, after the window problems.

edits.quote: To find the next label, inspect the first, second, and fourth cells: mark the next W if any is L, and L if all three are W.
edits.fix: This prints the update rule that is the heart of the periodicity argument. Ask instead: 'Why do the four labels before a pile decide its label? Which of them matter?'

edits.quote: Window starts at 0 / 7 / 1 / 8 ... Window after sliding
edits.fix: The interleaved row order and the 'Window after sliding' column (which just repeats the next row) make it unclear what to fill and when the problem is done. Use one simple slide sequence or drop the column.

edits.quote: Find another matching pair of four-label windows in your chart. Copy both windows, extend them by two labels, and compare the results.
edits.fix: This is unintentionally trivial: the chart already holds the labels after every window, so 'extend' is copying, and any windows at n and n+7 match. It never asks what a match implies. Rewrite: 'Explain why, once two windows match, the labels repeat forever. How many different four-label windows are possible? Must every rule's pattern repeat eventually?'

grades-4-5.summary: This is the deepest band, with a correct period-7 pattern for {1,3,4}, a remainder argument, the {1,3,5} parity contrast and the window/pigeonhole idea from the outline. It is over-directed: P5 hands over grouping by 7, P9 prints the update rule, and the 7-wide chart with 'compare the rows' gives away the period. P2 and P4 repeat P3, and P10 is trivial because the continuations are already in the chart.

overall.strongest: The grades 4-5 pages carry the outline's deepest ideas (backward induction, the period-7 pattern and why it persists, a rule change, and the window argument) with all expected answers mathematically correct.
overall.weakest: The K-1 pages give a quick child only about 18 minutes of work, and P4 and P6 print the leave-a-multiple-of-3 strategy before children can discover it.
